title: Love thy Book
author: Christopher Perrin
summary: Christopher Perrin argues from the classical and Christian tradition that love, not intellect alone, is the engine and the unifier of learning. Drawing on A.G. Sertillanges, Plato, Quintilian and Augustine, he claims that we think with our whole person (mind, body and soul) and that our thinking is only as healthy as our loves are ordered. He illustrates this with ordinary experience: exhaustion, hunger and pain wreck mental work, and so do disordered desires such as lust or the craving for online approval. He extends the point to teaching, insisting that students learn to love the lovely mainly by watching a teacher who loves it, so that a teacher who has stopped loving history should stop teaching it. The essay closes with the image of love as a dance hall with many doors (a book, a painting, a piece of music), where the only price of admission is love.
points: Perrin's central claim is that love is the source of unity between knowing and doing, so desire for knowledge and the practical ability to gain it grow together.
Because humans are a unity of mind, body and soul, we think with the whole person, which explains why fatigue, hunger and pain degrade academic work.
Disordered loves (he cites lust and the pursuit of online popularity) damage a student's capacity for precise thought just as surely as a lack of ability would.
Citing Quintilian, he holds that the best student, like the best orator, will be morally virtuous, so moral formation is not separate from intellectual formation.
The practical implication for teachers is to model love for the subject openly, since students are drawn into the lovely by seeing a teacher who already loves it.
quotes: Rather, since we humans are a unity of mind, body, and soul, we think with our whole person, our whole being.
Try working out a mental sum when you are exhausted, sick, or in acute pain. Imagine being presented with an algebra problem or ethical conundrum before your morning cup of coffee.
If our loves are ordered according to the good, then our various faculties are harmonized. Put another way, if we seek to do good and be good, we will also think well.

How can the 17-year-old boy addicted to pornography and racked by lust attend to the demands of precise calculations or careful distinctions required by chemistry, algebra, or the various dimensions of word play and allusion in great poetry?
There is no doubt in the Christian tradition that love makes the man and therefore makes the student and teacher.
If there is a formula for making this happen in a student, I know only one: display your own love for the lovely. When you stop loving history, stop teaching it.
Augustine is famous for saying we must order our loves in light of God’s love. He says in the Confessions, “My love is my weight, by it I am carried wherever I am carried.
